paper.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations

beats.narration: Your model returned perfectly valid JSON. That tells you almost nothing about whether the answer is right. New work puts a number on how far apart valid and right can sit.
beats.narration_template: Your model returned perfectly valid JSON. That tells you almost nothing about whether the answer is right. New work puts a number on how far apart valid and right can sit.

beats.narration: Teams use language models to extract fields, write queries and route requests. The output is parsed and stored, so a schema check feels like proof of quality. The authors argue that a parseable answer is necessary, yet it does not establish task correctness.
beats.narration_template: Teams use language models to extract fields, write queries and route requests. The output is parsed and stored, so a schema check feels like proof of quality. The authors argue that a parseable answer is necessary, yet it does not establish task correctness.

beats.narration: They built a benchmark that scores schema fit and task correctness separately: whether the output fits the schema, and whether it is right for the task. Business tasks ran through Python setups, with a shared model and an analysis plan frozen in advance. That produced a primary matrix of five thousand four hundred rows.

beats.narration: Overall schema validity came in at zero point six eight four, and mean automated quality at zero point six three eight. PydanticAI, LangGraph and DSPy stayed near the ceiling, with mean quality of zero point nine one to zero point nine four. The plain SDK, Agno and CrewAI landed substantially lower in this configuration.

beats.narration: The authors are careful here. These are findings about whole system configurations, not proof that a library feature causes better quality. The tasks are synthetic, the human audit packet is still unreviewed, and the benchmark is not a security or deployment certification.
